passage:
Supervisor's note, Dr Ganga, final-year projects, 22 January
Farhan has rewritten his literature review four times this term, never satisfied, and missed two internal deadlines. Last week we agreed to try something new: a fixed three-hour slot, after which he submits whatever solid version he has, with a separate list titled "Next time". Today he handed in the review on time. It is not perfect; two sections are thinner than they could be. But it is clear, well organised and complete, the best thing he has given me. His "Next time" list has four items, including "start citations earlier". He looked nervous handing it over, then visibly relieved when I said it was good.
My next step: we'll use the same time box for the methods chapter and go through his list together on Friday.

qa.q: What title did Farhan give his separate list?
qa.a: "Next time."

qa.q: Why did Farhan look nervous handing over the review, then relieved?
qa.a: Submitting something less than perfect felt risky after months of rewriting; hearing it was good showed him a solid version was enough.

qa.q: Which part of the plan keeps high standards without the paralysis?
qa.a: The "Next time" list, which records improvements for later so the current version can be finished within the three-hour slot.

qa.q: How does Dr Ganga see the new approach working?
qa.a: Dr Ganga sees the most complete work Farhan has produced, delivered on time, and plans to reuse the time box for the next chapter.

grounding: A supervisor records a student using a time limit to submit a solid version and listing improvements for next time.

passage:
Tuesday night
Did the thing Avni suggested. Gave myself till 9 p.m. for the marketing case study, no extensions. At 8:55 it was maybe 85% of what I wanted. The graphs could be prettier, and the conclusion is a bit short. The old me would've kept going till 3 a.m. and then submitted late, or not at all. Instead I hit submit. My heart pounded for a whole minute. Then I opened a new page and wrote "For next time": 1) start the graphs on day one, 2) outline the conclusion before writing, 3) ask Avni to read the draft. Weirdly, I feel lighter than after any assignment this year. I even had time to call home. Good enough, then better. That's the plan now.
Jomon

qa.q: What deadline did Jomon set for the case study?
qa.a: 9 p.m., no extensions.

qa.q: Why did Jomon's heart pound after hitting submit?
qa.a: Sending work that felt only 85% ready went against the old habit of polishing all night, so letting go felt scary even though it was the right choice.

qa.q: Which choice turned the unfinished parts into something useful?
qa.a: Writing a "For next time" list, so the weaker graphs and short conclusion became lessons rather than reasons to keep working.

qa.q: How might Avni feel reading the "For next time" list?
qa.a: Avni would probably be pleased the suggestion worked and happy to read the next draft, as the list asks.

grounding: A student sets a time limit, submits a solid version and notes improvements, keeping standards without paralysis.

passage: Payal, you asked why I looked so tired at your wedding. Honestly? That was the week of the quarterly report. I'd been rewriting the same executive summary for six days. Every time I read a sentence, I'd find something slightly off. Meanwhile Rohit on my team sent his section on day two, rough, and the director thanked him in front of everyone for being so quick. My section was better, I know it was. But it came in three days late, and by then the director had already built the presentation around Rohit's numbers. I skipped your mehendi to keep polishing. I haven't gone to bed before midnight in a month. And for what? The part I was so proud of got one line in the final deck. That's the real story, from your very tired friend Indu.

qa.q: How many days did Indu spend rewriting the executive summary?
qa.a: Six days.

qa.q: What does Indu feel about Rohit being thanked for speed?
qa.a: Indu feels frustrated and a bit bitter, believing the section was better but seeing the rough, early version win the credit.

qa.q: What choice could Indu try with the next report?
qa.a: Set a deadline to send a good draft early, as Rohit did, and polish only the most important parts afterwards.

qa.q: How might Payal feel hearing why Indu missed the mehendi?
qa.a: Payal may feel sad that work took Indu from the celebration, and worried about how tired a friend has been.

grounding: An adult polishes a report for days, delivers late, loses credit to a faster colleague and misses a friend's celebration.

passage: I'm Lakshmi, and I've shared a desk cluster with Bidisha at the advertising agency for a year. She's the most careful copywriter I've ever seen. She'll spend a whole afternoon choosing between two words. Clients love her lines, when they finally get them. But I've watched what it costs. Last month she delivered a campaign two days after the deadline because the tagline "wasn't there yet", and the account manager presented Sameer's faster, rougher version instead. She stays till ten most nights. She's stopped coming to Friday lunches. I don't know exactly what goes on in her head. I just noticed that when Sameer got praised, she smiled and said nothing, then went back to rewriting a line that already looked perfect to me.

qa.q: Why was Bidisha's campaign two days late?
qa.a: Because the tagline "wasn't there yet".

qa.q: What might Bidisha be feeling when she smiles and says nothing after Sameer is praised?
qa.a: She may feel hurt and frustrated but hide it, turning back to polishing as if more work could make up for the lost credit.

qa.q: What could Bidisha try, and how might Lakshmi help?
qa.a: Agree a "good enough" point for each line before the deadline, and let Lakshmi read drafts early so she can send them on time.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi experience Bidisha's perfectionism?
qa.a: Lakshmi admires the craft but misses her at Friday lunches, and sees the late nights and lost credit with quiet concern.

grounding: A colleague observes a careful copywriter whose rigid standards cost deadlines, credit, rest and friendships.

passage:
Monday: Nazia's audit summary was due to the partner by Wednesday. By evening she had a full draft, but the tables weren't aligned quite right, so she started reformatting. Bidisha, at the next desk, sent hers at six and left for badminton.
Wednesday: At midnight Nazia was still adjusting fonts. She messaged her mother that she'd miss the family dinner again. The partner emailed at nine the next morning: "Where is it?"
Friday: Bidisha's summary, sent on time, had gone to the client with the partner's praise. Nazia's arrived Thursday afternoon, polished to a shine. The partner replied with one word: "Thanks." That night Nazia sat in the office pantry, staring at the untouched tiffin her mother had packed, and couldn't remember the last time she'd played badminton.

qa.q: What did the partner email at nine on Thursday morning?
qa.a: "Where is it?"

qa.q: What might Nazia be feeling as she stares at the untouched tiffin?
qa.a: She seems deflated and lonely; days of polishing brought one word of thanks, while dinners with family and her old badminton slipped away.

qa.q: What was the turning point Nazia missed, and what could she do next time?
qa.a: Monday evening, when the full draft was ready; sending it then, with the table fixes noted, would have met the deadline.

qa.q: How might Nazia's mother feel about the missed dinners?
qa.a: Her mother may feel worried and a little sad, packing tiffins that go uneaten and missing her daughter at the family table.

grounding: Over a week an adult's rigid polishing of a report costs her the deadline, credit, family time and rest.

passage:
Sunday, late
Binita cancelled on me again, the third Sunday in a row. Her message said "still fixing the thesis chapter, sorry sorry". I went over with momos anyway. Her room was dark except for the laptop, and she had those grey circles under her eyes. She showed me the chapter. It was good, really good. She'd spent two days on the spacing of one table. I didn't argue. I just said, "Let me read it like a rough draft that only has to be good enough. Only to see if it makes sense. Nothing else." She hesitated so long I thought she'd say no. Then she turned the laptop to me. I read it while she ate. I found one real typo. She laughed, fixed it and sent it to her guide at 11 p.m. Then she fell asleep on the sofa.
Tenzin

qa.q: How long had Binita spent on the spacing of one table?
qa.a: Two days.

qa.q: Why did Binita hesitate so long before turning the laptop around?
qa.a: Letting someone see the chapter meant risking that its flaws would be noticed, and after days of polishing, that felt frightening.

qa.q: Which choice by Tenzin helped Binita send the chapter?
qa.a: Offering to read it only as a good-enough draft, and staying while she ate, so checking felt safe and limited.

qa.q: What was it like for Binita to have Tenzin there?
qa.a: With company and one small typo found, the imperfection felt survivable, and she could finally send it and sleep.

grounding: A friend notices someone cancelling plans and losing sleep over tiny flaws, and offers to read it as a good-enough draft.

passage: In Hoshangabad, Pankaj noticed his cousin Hrithik's lamp still on at two in the morning for the third night running. Hrithik taught at the government primary school and had to submit the annual activity report to the block office on Monday. He'd skipped the Saturday cricket match and the temple fair. "One photo is blurry, and the table has a spelling mistake I can't find," he said, rubbing his eyes. Pankaj sat on the charpai beside him. "Give it here. I'll read it like a first draft, not a final one. We'll fix only what's wrong." Hrithik hesitated, then handed it over. Pankaj found two small mistakes. They fixed them together in ten minutes. Hrithik looked at the finished file for a long time, then switched off the lamp.

qa.q: When did Hrithik have to submit the activity report?
qa.a: On Monday, to the block office.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik hesitate before handing the report to Pankaj?
qa.a: After three late nights chasing tiny flaws, he may have feared someone else would find more wrong with it.

qa.q: What choice by Pankaj ended the late nights?
qa.a: Reading the report as a first draft and fixing only what was actually wrong, together, which took ten minutes.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see his cousin's week?
qa.a: Pankaj notices the lamp at two in the morning and the skipped cricket and fair, and sees the strain before offering help.

grounding: A cousin notices a young teacher losing sleep and skipping plans over small flaws, and offers to check it as a draft.

passage: At her cousin's engagement in Bhilwara, Vandana had tried to join the older girls' conversation and said, too loudly, "Oh, I thought she was your mother!" about a woman who turned out to be the girl's elder sister. There was a pause, then laughter, then the talk moved on. But for Vandana, it didn't. Walking home past the stepwell, she replayed it. Lying on the roof that night, she replayed it again, each time a little worse. On Tuesday, grinding masala with her mother, she thought of a better line she could have said. By Wednesday she was sure the whole mohalla knew. When Madhuri asked why she'd gone so quiet, Vandana said, "I'm just trying to figure out how to fix it." But nothing she came up with fixed anything. It only stung more.

qa.q: What did Vandana say too loudly at the engagement?
qa.a: "Oh, I thought she was your mother!"

qa.q: Why does Vandana feel she is "trying to figure out how to fix it"?
qa.a: Replaying the moment feels like working on the problem, so it seems useful, even though each replay only makes the embarrassment sharper.

qa.q: What could help Vandana break the replay?
qa.a: Noticing that the talk moved on within seconds, and turning her attention to something absorbing when the memory returns, rather than rehearsing new lines.

qa.q: How might the older girls remember the moment?
qa.a: They probably laughed briefly and forgot it, unlike Vandana, who imagines the whole mohalla still talking about it.

grounding: A teenager replays an awkward remark at a family function for days, and the replaying deepens the sting.

passage: At Felix's sixteenth birthday party in Vancouver, Mei tried to make a joke about his new haircut. It came out wrong: "Did you lose a bet?" Felix laughed, sort of. Someone said, "Ouch." That was Saturday. By Wednesday, Mei had replayed it maybe a hundred times: in the shower, on the bus, in the middle of chemistry. She imagined Felix telling everyone. She imagined them all remembering it every time they saw her. She drafted three apology texts and deleted them all. Each replay felt like working out the problem, but each one made her face burn hotter. On Thursday Felix sat next to her at lunch and chatted about basketball as if nothing had happened. Mei barely heard a word.

qa.q: What joke did Mei make about Felix's haircut?
qa.a: "Did you lose a bet?"

qa.q: Why did Mei keep replaying the joke?
qa.a: Each replay felt like solving the problem, as if thinking it through enough would undo it, but it only made her more embarrassed.

qa.q: What could Mei try on Thursday instead of barely listening?
qa.a: Notice that Felix is acting normally, join the basketball chat, and, if it still bothers her, say one short "sorry about the haircut joke" and let it go.

qa.q: How does Felix seem to see the moment by Thursday?
qa.a: Felix seems to have moved on completely, chatting about basketball as if nothing happened, unlike Mei.

grounding: A teenager replays an awkward party joke for days, imagining everyone remembers it, and the sting deepens.

passage: At the school's Class 10 farewell, Chandrika had been asked to say a few words on stage, and in her nervousness she called their class teacher "Mummy" into the microphone. The hall exploded with laughter. The teacher laughed too, kindly. Three days later, Chandrika still hadn't stopped replaying it. In the library she stared at the same page. In the corridor, every laugh seemed to be about her. She went over what she should have said, sentence by sentence, as if she could solve it. On Monday the school counsellor, Mr Amandeep, found her alone on the steps. "You look like you're carrying something heavy," he said. Chandrika said, "I'm just thinking it through." "How many times have you thought it through?" She didn't know. Too many.

qa.q: What did Chandrika call the class teacher into the microphone?
qa.a: "Mummy."

qa.q: Why does Chandrika say she is "just thinking it through"?
qa.a: Going over it sentence by sentence feels like solving the problem, so it seems sensible, even as it keeps the embarrassment fresh.

qa.q: Which question from Mr Amandeep might help Chandrika step out of the loop?
qa.a: "How many times have you thought it through?", because it shows her that the replaying has become a loop rather than a solution.

qa.q: How did the class teacher seem to react to the slip?
qa.a: The teacher laughed kindly along with the hall, suggesting it was a warm, funny moment rather than something to hold against her.

grounding: A teenager replays a slip on stage for days, and the rehearsing feels like problem solving but deepens the embarrassment.

passage: Rehana failed her cost accounting paper, and for two weeks she didn't stop asking why. In the hostel room in Lucknow, she'd lie on the bed going over it: was it the night before, when she couldn't sleep? Was she just bad at numbers? Did it mean she'd chosen the wrong course, the wrong life? Every answer led to another question. Zainab, her roommate, tried to help. "Want to look at the paper together and see which questions went wrong?" "Not yet," Rehana said. "I need to understand why first." The re-exam form sat on her desk, unfilled. Her tea went cold every evening. She felt as if she was thinking very hard, getting nowhere, and getting heavier.

qa.q: What sat on Rehana's desk, unfilled?
qa.a: The re-exam form.

qa.q: Why does Rehana say "I need to understand why first"?
qa.a: Searching for the cause feels responsible and necessary, as if a plan can't come until she knows what the failure says about her.

qa.q: What small step could break Rehana's loop?
qa.a: Accepting Zainab's offer to go through the paper question by question and filling in the re-exam form, turning "why" into "what next".

qa.q: How might Zainab feel when the offer is put off?
qa.a: Zainab may feel helpless and worried, watching a friend sink further while a practical way forward sits unused.

grounding: A student who failed a paper keeps asking why and what it means about her, without making any plan, and her mood sinks.

passage:
"Raghav, you've been lying there since lunch."
"Thinking, bhaiya."
Hemant sat at the foot of his younger brother's bed. "About the maths paper?"
"About why I failed it. Was it the new professor? Was it me? Maybe I'm just not an engineering person. Maybe I never was, and Papa pushed me, and I went along, and now..."
"Raghav."
"...and if I'm not an engineering person, what am I? Why couldn't I see it before?"
"How long have you been going round like this?"
"Since the results. Nine days."
"And what's the plan?"
Raghav blinked. "Plan?"
"For the supplementary. It's in six weeks."
"I haven't... I'm still figuring out why."
Hemant held up the syllabus. "What if we figure out which chapters first?"

qa.q: When is the supplementary exam?
qa.a: In six weeks.

qa.q: Why does Raghav blink at the word "plan"?
qa.a: He has been so caught up in why he failed and what it says about him that doing something next hadn't even occurred to him.

qa.q: What choice does Hemant offer to break the loop?
qa.a: Looking at which chapters to study first, moving from endless why-questions to one concrete step toward the supplementary.

qa.q: How does Hemant see his younger brother's nine days?
qa.a: Hemant sees him lying in bed going round in circles, and gently steers him to a plan rather than joining the why-questions.

grounding: A student who failed a paper keeps asking why and what it says about him, with no plan until his brother asks for one.

passage: After I failed Organic Chemistry II last semester, I spent a whole month inside one question: why? I'd lie awake building theories. Maybe I wasn't smart enough. Maybe I'd been lucky in first year and this was the truth coming out. Maybe something was wrong with how my brain worked. Each theory made me feel worse, but I kept at it, because it felt like work, like I was being responsible. Sarika, my lab partner, finally asked, "Lavanya, after all this thinking, what are you going to do differently?" I opened my mouth and nothing came out. I had a hundred reasons and not one plan. That night I wrote three: office hours every week, practice reaction problems daily, redo the paper with Sarika. The why can wait. I feel lighter already.

qa.q: What three steps did Lavanya write that night?
qa.a: Office hours every week, practice reaction problems daily, and redo the paper with Sarika.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya keep building theories even though each made things worse?
qa.a: It felt like responsible work, as if understanding the cause had to come first, so stopping seemed careless.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Sarika asking what Lavanya would do differently; it exposed a hundred reasons but no plan, and led to three concrete steps.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel being part of the plan?
qa.a: Sarika may feel glad that the question helped, and happy to redo the paper together as a partner.

grounding: A student stuck asking why the paper was failed realises the thinking has no plan, and writes concrete steps.

passage: For the sixth evening in a row, Dilnaz called Zeenat on the walk home from the metro, and for the sixth time they went over the job interview. What the panel had asked. They weren't solving anything; they were walking the same circle. When Dilnaz started again, "I just keep thinking, if I'd said...", Zeenat waited for a pause and asked gently, "Dilu, what's one small thing that might help this week?" Dilnaz was quiet. Then: "Maybe ask the panel for feedback?" "That sounds like a good one."

qa.q: How many evenings in a row had Dilnaz called about the interview?
qa.a: Six evenings.

qa.q: What did Zeenat notice about how the calls made them both feel?
qa.a: That after every call Dilnaz sounded worse, not better, and so did Zeenat; the talk brought no relief.

qa.q: Which choice by Zeenat changed the direction of the call?
qa.a: Waiting for a pause and gently asking for one small helpful step, which led Dilnaz to think of asking the panel for feedback.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel after naming a step?
qa.a: Dilnaz may feel a little lighter and more in control, having moved from reliving the interview to something to do.

grounding: A friend notices that rehashing a disappointment brings no relief and gently asks what small step might help.

passage: For about a month last winter, I was Shalini's sounding board, and I thought I was being a good friend. Her research grant had been rejected, and every lunch we went over it again: the reviewer's harsh comment, the budget section, whether her supervisor had really read it. I'd nod, add my own theories, get angry on her behalf. We'd leave the canteen and she'd look greyer than when we sat down. So would I. One day I realised we'd said the exact same sentences three lunches in a row. The talk wasn't bringing any relief. The next time she started, I asked, as gently as I could, "Is there one tiny thing you could do about it today?" She stared at me, then said, "I could email the grants office about resubmitting." She did it before we finished our tea. I'm Lalremsiami, and I still listen. I just ask that question sooner.

qa.q: What did Shalini decide to do after the question?
qa.a: Email the grants office about resubmitting.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami think the lunches were good friendship at first?
qa.a: Listening, adding theories and getting angry on Shalini's behalf felt like support, and it was hard to see from inside that it was keeping them both stuck.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Lalremsiami helps?
qa.a: Noticing the same sentences three lunches in a row, then asking about one tiny thing to do that day, which led to action within one cup of tea.

qa.q: How might Shalini have felt when asked about a small step?
qa.a: Shalini seemed surprised at first, then relieved to turn a month of hurt into one concrete action.

grounding: A friend realises that rehashing a grant rejection brings no relief and gently asks what small step might help now.

passage: Since the argument with his manager on Monday, Bao's mind had been looping every evening in his London flat: what he should have said, what she'd think of him, whether he'd be let go. On Thursday he caught himself mid-loop in the kitchen and tried what his flatmate Kwame had suggested. He wrote the thought on a sticky note: "Worried she thinks I'm difficult." He set a timer for fifteen minutes and let himself think about it properly, even jotting one thing he could say to her on Friday. When the timer rang, he stuck the note on the fridge and started cooking pho from scratch: chopping, stirring, tasting. By the time the broth was ready, his head was quiet. Kwame, tasting it, said, "If the loops ever get constant or really dark, talk to someone professional, yeah?" Bao nodded. "I will."

qa.q: What did Bao write on the sticky note?
qa.a: "Worried she thinks I'm difficult."

qa.q: Why did the looping feel hard for Bao to stop on his own?
qa.a: He was worried about his job and his manager's opinion, so going over it felt necessary, as if the next replay might settle it.

qa.q: Which steps helped Bao break the loop that evening?
qa.a: Writing the thought down, giving it fifteen timed minutes with one action for Friday, then cooking something absorbing.

qa.q: Why might Kwame mention talking to a professional?
qa.a: Kwame cares about Bao and knows that if the loops become constant or dark, a trained person can help more than tricks alone.

grounding: An adult notices rumination, writes the thought down, gives it a set time, then cooks, with a friend noting when to seek professional help.

passage: At the software firm in Chennai, Karthik booked a slot with Sabina, the in-house counsellor, after two weeks of replaying a failed product demo every night. "I lie there going over it," he said. "What went wrong, what they think of me. It never ends." Sabina nodded. "Let's try something. When it starts, write the thought down, word for word. Give it fifteen minutes, a real appointment, at seven. Then do something that needs your hands and head, like cooking or a walk." She added, "And if the thoughts start coming all the time, or turn really dark, come back to me straight away or see a doctor. That's important." That evening at seven Karthik wrote, "I embarrassed myself in front of the client." He thought about it for fifteen minutes, then went for a brisk walk round the lake. He was asleep by eleven.

qa.q: What did Karthik write at seven that evening?
qa.a: "I embarrassed myself in front of the client."

qa.q: Why had the replaying felt endless to Karthik?
qa.a: He kept trying to work out what went wrong and what the client thought, and with no set limit the thoughts just circled every night.

qa.q: Which parts of Sabina's plan helped Karthik sleep?
qa.a: Writing the thought down, giving it a fixed fifteen-minute slot, then taking a brisk walk, so the worry had a place and an end.

qa.q: Why does Sabina stress coming back if the thoughts become constant or dark?
qa.a: Sabina wants Karthik to know the simple routine has limits, and that ongoing or dark thoughts deserve professional help straight away.

grounding: A counsellor teaches an adult to write the thought down, time-box it and then do something absorbing, with a note on when to seek help.

passage:
Dear Kalyani,
You asked how I'm doing since the shop closed. Honestly, the first weeks were bad. I kept going over it at night: the rent, the loan, what everyone in the para must be saying. My mind wouldn't stop. So I tried something a doctor friend suggested. When the loop starts, I write the thought in a small notebook, exactly as it sounds in my head. Then I give it twenty minutes, sitting at the table after dinner, to think it through properly. When the time's up, I close the notebook and do something with my hands. Mostly I cook. Last night I made your favourite shorshe ilish, badly. It helps. Not every night, but most. And I promised Ma that if it gets constant or very dark, I'll go and see someone properly. I will.
Your brother,
Arnab

qa.q: How long does Arnab give the thought each evening?
qa.a: Twenty minutes, sitting at the table after dinner.

qa.q: Why were the first weeks after the shop closed so hard for Arnab?
qa.a: Worry about the rent, the loan and what people were saying kept circling at night, and going over it felt necessary but brought no rest.

qa.q: Which steps from the letter could someone else try?
qa.a: Writing the looping thought down exactly, giving it a fixed short time, then doing something absorbing with the hands, like cooking.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Kalyani may feel relieved to hear the routine helps most nights, touched by the ilish, and reassured by the promise made to Ma.

grounding: An adult breaks nightly rumination by writing thoughts down, time-boxing them and cooking, and promises to seek help if it worsens.

passage: In the dark of his room in São Paulo, Emil, who was nine, couldn't stop the what-ifs. What if he failed the maths test tomorrow? What if Mamãe's bus crashed on the way home from her night shift? What if she got sick like Vovó? Each question pulled another behind it, like carriages on a train. His heart thumped. Papai was already asleep. Emil crept to the kitchen, where his mother, Priscila, was making tea before leaving. "I can't sleep. What if something happens to you?" Priscila knelt and held his hands. "I'm careful, and I always come home. Let's do our thing." They did: three slow breaths, a glass of water, one page of his dinosaur book in her voice. Back in bed, the train of questions slowed. He was asleep before she left.

qa.q: What did Emil and Priscila do together before bed?
qa.a: Three slow breaths, a glass of water and one page of his dinosaur book.

qa.q: Why did the what-ifs keep coming for Emil?
qa.a: His worry was trying to get ready for every danger, the test and his mother's safety, but each question only set off another alarm.

qa.q: What helped Emil settle, and why did it work?
qa.a: Priscila's calm reassurance and their familiar routine, which gave his body and mind something steady to hold onto.

qa.q: What is it like for Priscila to hear Emil's worry before her night shift?
qa.a: She may feel tender and a little torn about leaving, but she stays calm so her steadiness can quiet his fear.

grounding: A child's night-time what-ifs about a test and his mother are calmed by reassurance and a familiar routine.

passage: At the residential school in Panchgani, lights-out was at nine, but Omkar, who was eleven, lay awake in the dormitory most nights. What if he failed the half-yearly exams and had to go home in shame? What if Aai fell ill while he was far away? What if the Sunday phone call didn't come? His stomach churned. One night Tushar sir, the house warden, found him sitting up in bed. Omkar whispered it all in a rush. Tushar sir didn't laugh. "Those what-ifs feel like getting ready for trouble, don't they? Mostly they just ring alarm bells." He helped Omkar write the worries on a slip to drop in the worry box by the door, and promised he could phone Aai the next evening. Then he sat nearby while Omkar breathed slowly. Omkar was asleep before ten.

qa.q: Where did Omkar put the slip with his worries?
qa.a: In the worry box by the door.

qa.q: Why did Omkar's stomach churn at night?
qa.a: Far from home, he kept imagining failing and his Aai falling ill; the worry felt like preparing but only made him more alarmed.

qa.q: Which choices by Tushar sir helped Omkar sleep?
qa.a: Listening without laughing, naming the what-ifs as alarm bells, using the worry box, promising a call to Aai and sitting nearby during slow breathing.

qa.q: How might Aai feel if she knew about Omkar's nights?
qa.a: Aai would probably feel moved and a little worried, and glad that someone at the school noticed and comforted him.

grounding: A boarding-school child's night-time what-ifs are eased by a warden's calm reassurance and a simple routine.

passage: I'm Sudha, Mohit's older sister, and we share a room. Lately I've noticed he doesn't sleep. After lights-off he turns and turns, and sometimes he whispers questions into the dark: "What if I forget my lines in the school play? What if Amma doesn't come back from Nani's?" Amma had gone to Nani's for a week because Nani was unwell. I don't know everything he's thinking, but his voice sounds tight, as if he's holding his breath. On Tuesday I told Amma on the phone. She called him every night after that at eight, the same time, and told him about her day. Papa started reading with him after the call. By Friday, Mohit was asleep before I'd finished brushing my teeth.

qa.q: What time did Amma call Mohit each night?
qa.a: At eight, the same time every night.

qa.q: What does Mohit's tight voice suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He seems frightened, worried about the play and about Amma not returning, and the questions keep him on alert instead of letting him rest.

qa.q: Which choices helped Mohit sleep by Friday?
qa.a: Sudha telling Amma, Amma's steady nightly call, and Papa reading afterwards, a calm routine with reassurance built in.

qa.q: How does Sudha experience her brother's worry?
qa.a: Sudha notices his restless turning and whispered questions, can't be sure what he's thinking, and cares enough to tell Amma.

grounding: An older sister notices her brother's night-time what-ifs about their mother and a routine of calls and reading calms him.

passage: The Class 10 board exams were four days away, and the power in Lalremsiami's part of Aizawl kept going off in the evenings. By candlelight she opened her science guide and instead started a list in her head: what if the paper was long, what if she blanked on chemical equations, what if she scored less than her cousin, what if the result ruined her chances of the science stream. An hour passed. She had read half a page. When Shalini called to ask how revision was going, Lalremsiami said, "I've been thinking about the exam all evening." It sounded almost like studying. But when she put the phone down, the guide was still open at the same page, and the candle had burned halfway down.

qa.q: How much had Lalremsiami read after an hour?
qa.a: Half a page.

qa.q: Why did "thinking about the exam all evening" feel almost like studying?
qa.a: Worrying about every way it could go wrong felt responsible and serious, so it seemed like preparation even though no revision was happening.

qa.q: What small step could Lalremsiami take the next evening?
qa.a: Set a short timer by the candle and revise just the chemical equations, noting any new worry on paper to come back to later.

qa.q: How might Shalini read Lalremsiami's answer on the phone?
qa.a: Shalini might assume she was revising hard, not realising the evening had gone to worry rather than study.

grounding: A teenager spends her revision time imagining every way the exam could go wrong, and barely starts studying.

passage: In their flat in Tolichowki, Rehana sat at her desk with the physics textbook open and her head full of the future. If she did badly in the pre-board, she wouldn't get into the good junior college. Then no engineering seat. Then Abbu's disappointment, and the neighbours asking. Every time she tried to start a numerical, another what-if arrived. By nine she had solved one problem. Her younger sister Zainab came in with chai. "You've been studying so hard," Zainab said admiringly. "I've been worrying so hard," Rehana corrected, half laughing, half near tears. "It feels like the same thing. It isn't." Zainab set down the chai and looked at the single solved problem. "Want me to time you for fifteen minutes? Just one chapter."

qa.q: How many problems had Rehana solved by nine?
qa.a: One problem.

qa.q: What does Rehana mean by "It feels like the same thing. It isn't"?
qa.a: She realises that worrying about the future feels as heavy and responsible as studying, but it has taken the place of actually doing problems.

qa.q: Which choice offered by Zainab could help Rehana start?
qa.a: A timed fifteen-minute session on one chapter, which shrinks the task and gives her mind something to do instead of worrying.

qa.q: How does Zainab see her sister's evening at first, and what changes?
qa.a: Zainab first thinks Rehana has been studying hard, then sees the single solved problem and offers practical help.

grounding: A teenager's worry about exams and her future replaces study, and her sister offers a short timed start.

passage:
"Varun, dinner. You've been in your room since four."
"Coming, Papa. I'm studying."
Nitin came into his son's room and looked at the desk. The maths book was open at the first page of the chapter. Beside it lay a sheet covered in writing.
"What's this?"
"Things that could go wrong in the exam." Varun didn't look up. "If the paper's long. If I get the calculus questions. If my pen stops. If I get sick. If I don't get into the science stream..."
"That's a long list."
"I need to be prepared."
"How many sums have you done?"
Varun was quiet. "None yet."
Nitin sat on the bed. "Worrying feels like work, beta. But the list isn't doing the sums. Let's pick the first three questions of the chapter. After dinner, together."

qa.q: How many sums had Varun done?
qa.a: None yet.

qa.q: Why does Varun say "I need to be prepared" about his list?
qa.a: Listing every possible problem feels responsible, as if imagining disasters is getting ready for them, so it seems like useful work.

qa.q: What choice does Nitin suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Doing the first three questions together after dinner, which turns the worry into a small, concrete action.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel seeing the long list and no sums?
qa.a: Nitin is likely concerned but calm, recognising that his son is anxious rather than lazy, and choosing to help rather than scold.

grounding: A teenager lists every way an exam could go wrong instead of studying, and his father steers him to three sums.

passage: In their house in Rewari, Kashish, eighteen, had started doing something strange. Before bed she checked the gas knob, then the front door latch, then the gas again. She had never done that before her brother Sachin came home to study for his civil services prelims. Sachin checked everything twice, sometimes three times, and asked her whether she'd locked the scooter or switched off the geyser, in a tight, fast voice. The whole house had started to hum with it. One night their mother saw Kashish at the gas knob and sat them both down. She said plainly that Sachin was anxious about his exam, that it wasn't anyone's fault, and that there would be one routine now: Ma would lock up at ten, once, and nobody else would check. Sachin agreed to talk to a counsellor. Kashish slept better that week.

qa.q: Who would lock up at ten under the new routine?
qa.a: Ma, once, and nobody else would check.

qa.q: Why had Kashish started checking the gas and the latch?
qa.a: Sachin's tight, repeated questions filled the house with tension, and she picked up his alarm without deciding to.

qa.q: Which choices by their mother lightened the house?
qa.a: Naming Sachin's anxiety honestly and without blame, setting one clear locking routine, and Sachin agreeing to see a counsellor.

qa.q: What was it like for Kashish living with Sachin's worry?
qa.a: The house seemed to hum with tension, and she found herself copying his checking, until the new routine let her sleep better.

grounding: A younger sister picks up her anxious brother's checking habits, and clear routines and honest talk ease it.

passage: In the flat in Johannesburg, Siddiq noticed he'd started checking his phone for university messages every ten minutes, even though his own exams were months away. It had begun when his older brother Thabo's finals started. Thabo paced the kitchen at night, refreshed the results page, and asked Siddiq three times whether he'd set the alarm, whether the lights were off, whether he'd heard anything. The tension crept into Siddiq like cold. One Sunday their father called a family meeting at the kitchen table. "We're all jumpy," he said honestly. "Thabo is stressed, and it's catching." They agreed: dinner at seven, phones in a basket till eight, and Thabo would check the results page only once, in the morning. Siddiq felt his shoulders drop for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: What did the family agree to at the kitchen table?
qa.a: Dinner at seven, phones in a basket till eight, and Thabo checking the results page only once, in the morning.

qa.q: How did Thabo's stress affect Siddiq, and what shows it?
qa.a: Siddiq became tense and watchful too; checking his phone every ten minutes for exams months away shows he had picked up his brother's vigilance.

qa.q: Which choice by their father helped most, and why?
qa.a: Saying honestly that Thabo's stress was catching and setting clear shared routines, which named the problem without blame and gave everyone limits.

qa.q: How might Thabo feel about the new routine?
qa.a: Thabo might find checking only once hard at first, but may also feel relieved to have a limit and to know his family understands.

grounding: A younger brother picks up his anxious older brother's checking, until honest talk and clear routines ease the whole family.

passage: At the college counselling centre, Jagdish, a first-year, sat twisting his cap. "It's not me who's anxious," he began. "It's my sister Preeti. She's in final year here, placements. She calls me every night, asks if I've locked the room, if I've backed up my files, if I've checked the notice board. Now I do it too. I checked my laptop backup five times yesterday." The counsellor nodded. "Worry can travel through a family, even at a distance. It's nobody's fault." Together they made a plan: one fixed call time with Preeti, eight o'clock, ten minutes; one backup a day, at night; and an honest talk with Preeti about what the calls were doing to him. "Would you like her to come to a session too?" the counsellor asked. Jagdish nodded, relieved.

qa.q: How many times did Jagdish check his laptop backup yesterday?
qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: Why was Jagdish relieved at the end of the session?
qa.a: He learned that the checking he had picked up from his sister was understandable and nobody's fault, and he had a plan that included Preeti.

qa.q: Which parts of the plan could lighten the worry for both siblings?
qa.a: A fixed short call time, one backup a day, and an honest talk with Preeti, possibly in a shared session.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel when she hears what the calls were doing to Jagdish?
qa.a: Preeti may be surprised and sorry, not having realised her worry was spreading, and perhaps relieved to get support too.

grounding: A first-year student picks up his anxious sister's checking habits and works with a counsellor on routines and honest talk.
